content: Efforts are being made to conduct targeted outreach in high-risk areas during peak activity periods. These initiatives aim to promote the use of harm reduction services, distribute condoms, provide prevention information, and offer referrals to appropriate services. Public health centers and hospitals are closely integrated into this work, delivering both therapeutic and preventive services, such as Methadone Maintenance Therapy (MMT) and Needle and Syringe Programs (NSP), alongside safe injecting practices education. Strong partnerships have been established with law enforcement, the National Narcotics Board, the Ministry of Social Affairs, and the justice system to engage key stakeholders and duty bearers. Program activity data is collected monthly from all partners, and an annual behavioral and client satisfaction survey is conducted among program participants. This survey includes anonymous self-administered questionnaires addressing HIV testing history, serostatus, and satisfaction with community-based organizations (CBOs) and health services. In 2013, the HCPI supported 18 CBOs across eight provinces, providing services to over 14,000 clients. Additionally, 6,000 clients accessed services at 103 HCPI-supported government health centers (Puskesmas) and four government hospitals. Initially hesitant, the Ministry of Health (MoH) has now taken responsibility for NSPs but must commit to funding the millions of needles and syringes required annually. The MoH also increasingly funds MMT, ensuring its availability at numerous government health facilities. The Muslim Education and Welfare Association (MEWA) provides HIV prevention services and drug dependency treatment in Mombasa and Kilifi counties in Kenya. The project focuses on improving access to HIV prevention by offering clean needles and syringes, treatment, care, and socio-economic support services. Advocacy for opioid substitution therapy (OST) and the human rights of key populations is also a priority. A specific focus is placed on reuniting female drug users, many of whom live on the streets, with their families to support care engagement and retention. Free meals are provided as an incentive for service uptake, along with harm reduction services, reproductive health, and basic social services. Clients on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and tuberculosis (TB) treatment are offered free accommodations to support adherence. Entrepreneurship training, job placement opportunities, and referrals to government micro-financing programs are also available. MEWA builds trust with clients through consistent contact, strong referral systems, and community-based mobile services. Support is extended to the children of drug users, including temporary custodial care, health, nutritional, material, and psychosocial support. Family reunification has been achieved for half of MEWA’s clients. Outreach services and individualized tracking have increased service coverage for female drug users in the project area from 36% to 84%. Despite these achievements, challenges persist. Resistance to NSPs from law enforcement, due to perceptions that they promote drug use and crime, remains a barrier. Current laws do not align with new national guidelines and policies aimed at improving service delivery to key populations. MEWA addresses these issues through outreach, community dialogue, and training workshops for police officials, promoting human rights and dispelling myths about harm reduction services. The physical presence of outreach workers in high-risk areas fosters connections between the community, law enforcement, drug users, and MEWA staff. SIDC, a non-profit organization in Lebanon, has provided harm reduction services since 1996 and outreach interventions since 1999. Through comprehensive service delivery paired with outreach and advocacy, SIDC aims to scale up services, increase community uptake, and support retention in care. In 2010, SIDC launched Escale, the first drop-in center (DIC) in the Middle East for people who inject drugs (PWID). Escale offers harm reduction interventions, including HIV testing and counseling (HTC), needle and syringe programs, OST, psychosocial support, and legal assistance. Advocacy efforts counter stigma and discrimination, promote drug law reform, and encourage referrals to treatment centers instead of incarceration. Escale collaborates with the Middle East and North Africa Harm Reduction Association (MENAHRA) and other agencies to train stakeholders and service providers, enhancing understanding and tolerance of the PWID community. From 2010 to 2012, Escale reached approximately 1,600 PWID, primarily aged 20–35 years. However, OST is not free in Lebanon, limiting access for many in the PWID community. Recruitment and retention of NSP outreach workers remain challenging due to difficult-to-access hotspots, fear of police, and long-term alienation among drug users. Espolea, a youth-led organization in Mexico City, established a Drug Policy and Harm Reduction Program in 2008. They use online and face-to-face communication channels to provide practical, objective information about drugs and risk reduction to young people aged 15–29 years. Outreach is most effective at events where young people use drugs, such as music festivals and cultural gatherings. Espolea sets up safe spaces at these events to disseminate pragmatic materials emphasizing risks, harms, and safer practices. Workshops are also conducted in schools and communities with at-risk youth. Social media platforms, blogs, and printed materials are used to engage young people and provide information on nightlife, alcohol consumption, risky sexual behaviors, and HIV/STIs. The Nai Zindagi Trust in Pakistan has provided evidence-based services to street-based PWID, their families, and children for 25 years. They collaborate with the public health system to avoid creating parallel services, with 60% of services delivered by partner organizations. Nai Zindagi prioritizes outreach over facility-based approaches and involves PWID community members in program design and implementation. Comprehensive harm reduction services, including NSPs, HIV/STI prevention, and ART adherence programs, are offered. Skills training and employment opportunities are also available. A real-time management information system monitors service delivery and trends to adapt interventions to actual needs. Médecins du Monde (MdM) in Tanzania provides harm reduction services with a focus on women and critical enablers for service uptake. Services include NSPs, referrals to OST, income-generating activities, and legal support. MdM also supports the establishment of harm reduction committees and shelters for women and children. Continuous dialogue with authorities and sensitization sessions for police, health providers, and journalists are key elements of their work. Since 2011, over 6,000 people who use drugs have received harm reduction services, and more than 2,000 stakeholders have been trained in harm reduction approaches. In Ukraine, NGOs led by the International HIV/AIDS Alliance have provided harm reduction services since 2000, reaching up to 23% of the estimated PWID population by 2007. Peer-Driven Interventions (PDI) have extended services to underserved groups, including women and adolescents. Pharmacies have been involved as secondary outlets for distributing injecting instruments and prevention commodities, increasing program coverage by up to 10% in certain areas. Rapid HIV testing and case management approaches have reduced the time between HIV acquisition and treatment enrollment, improving harm reduction coverage and meeting the specific needs of PWID sub-populations.
